subject: feminism
title: Taiwan's women's movement: from New Feminism under martial law to the Domestic Violence Prevention Act
dek: In the early 1970s Annette Lu began writing about 'New Feminism' in a Taiwan still under martial law. Over the next three decades a small circle of writers became a movement, and a series of shocking cases about violence against women pushed Taiwan to rewrite its family law and pass some of the strongest gender-equality laws in Asia.
era: 1971 to 2004, with later effects to the present
honesty: This lesson keeps to events, laws and dates that are documented in Wikipedia's articles on feminism in Taiwan, the Awakening Foundation, Annette Lu and Peng Wan-ru, and in the Chinese-language articles on the Deng Ru-wen case and the Domestic Violence Prevention Act. Where historians disagree, for example on whether Taiwan's 1998 law was really 'the first in Asia', the lesson says so instead of picking one side. It does not quote people directly, because I could not verify exact wording in time.

timeline.label: Martial law begins
timeline.detail: Martial law is declared in Taiwan in May 1949 and lasts until July 1987. Independent civic organizations, including independent women's groups, are tightly restricted for nearly four decades.

timeline.label: Annette Lu starts the first organized women's-rights effort
timeline.detail: Lu Hsiu-lien (Annette Lu), a lawyer trained in Taiwan and the United States, begins public talks and writing on 'New Feminism' (新女性主義), the starting point of the modern movement.

timeline.label: Women are about 41.5% of the workforce
timeline.detail: Rapid industrialization pulls women into factories and offices; women's labour force participation rises from about 32.6% in 1966 to about 41.5% in 1973.

timeline.label: Kaohsiung Incident; Lu is imprisoned
timeline.detail: After the December 1979 Kaohsiung (Formosa) Incident, Lu is arrested with other opposition figures. She serves about five and a half years and is released in 1985.

timeline.label: Awakening magazine is founded
timeline.detail: Lee Yuan-chen and other associates of Lu found the Awakening publishing house and its magazine (婦女新知), the only independent group openly pressing for gender equality until martial law ends.

timeline.label: Martial law ends; Awakening becomes a foundation
timeline.detail: Martial law is lifted in July 1987. In November Awakening converts into the Awakening Foundation. The same year, 57 women working at the National Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall challenge rules forcing them to leave at age 30 or on pregnancy, and the Huaxi Street march protests the trafficking of young girls into prostitution.

timeline.label: Gender Equality in Employment bill drafted
timeline.detail: Awakening introduces a draft gender equality in employment bill. It takes twelve years to pass.

timeline.label: The Deng Ru-wen case
timeline.detail: In late 1993 in Banqiao, Deng Ru-wen kills her husband after years of severe abuse. Women's groups and human-rights groups support her, and she is sentenced to three years in prison. The case makes domestic violence a national issue.

timeline.label: Constitutional Interpretation No. 365
timeline.detail: The Council of Grand Justices rules that the Civil Code clause giving fathers priority in decisions about children violates constitutional equality, forcing family-law reform.

timeline.label: Family law reform and the murder of Peng Wan-ru
timeline.detail: The Civil Code's custody rules are revised. On 30 November 1996 Peng Wan-ru, head of the DPP's women's affairs department, disappears in Kaohsiung after taking a taxi; the same day her proposal to reserve a quarter of elected party seats for women passes.

timeline.label: Mass marches against violent crime; Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act
timeline.detail: Peng's murder and other high-profile cases bring large demonstrations in May 1997. A sexual assault prevention law is passed in 1997, and Taipei abolishes licensed prostitution in September.

timeline.label: Domestic Violence Prevention Act
timeline.detail: On 24 June 1998 Taiwan passes the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (家庭暴力防治法), which introduces civil protection orders and requires local governments to set up domestic violence prevention centers.

timeline.label: Annette Lu becomes vice president; Yeh Yung-chih dies
timeline.detail: Lu serves as vice president from 2000 to 2008. In April 2000 a gender-nonconforming junior high student, Yeh Yung-chih, is found dying in a school bathroom, a case that shapes the later education law.

timeline.label: Gender Equality in Employment Act
timeline.detail: Passed in 2001 and in force from 2002, it bans discrimination in hiring, pay and promotion and creates rights such as parental leave. It is renamed the Gender Equality in Employment (Work) Act in a 2007 amendment.

timeline.label: Gender Equity Education Act
timeline.detail: Co-drafted with help from Awakening, the act requires schools to teach gender equity and to protect students of every gender identity and sexual orientation.

timeline.label: Tsai Ing-wen elected president
timeline.detail: Taiwan elects its first woman president, a symbolic endpoint many writers connect to the movement's earlier work on women in politics.

fun_fact.title: A movement that began as a magazine
fun_fact.text: Because independent associations were almost impossible to register under martial law, the core of Taiwan's women's movement in the 1980s was legally a publishing house. Awakening could only become a foundation in November 1987, four months after martial law ended.

sections.title: Before the movement: women's work grows, but law and politics stay closed

blocks.text: In the 1960s and 1970s Taiwan industrialized very quickly. Export factories in electronics, textiles and plastics hired large numbers of young women, and women's share of the workforce rose from about a third in the mid-1960s to over two-fifths by 1973. Women were earning money, but the law still treated the family as something run by the husband.

The Civil Code, written in the Republic of China in the 1930s, gave the husband and father priority in many family decisions. When parents disagreed about a child, the father's decision prevailed. A wife was generally expected to live where her husband lived. Property acquired during marriage was often treated as the husband's. These rules were not only on paper. They shaped what happened in divorce, in custody disputes and in cases of violence, because a woman who left an abusive husband could lose both her home and her children.

At the same time, Taiwan had been under martial law since 1949. The government restricted new political parties, newspapers and civic associations. Official women's organizations existed, but they were linked to the ruling Kuomintang and focused on supporting the state and the family. An independent feminist movement would have to find space inside these limits.

Annette Lu, a lawyer who had studied law at National Taiwan University and then in the United States, began writing and speaking about what she called New Feminism in the early 1970s. Her arguments were deliberately moderate. She did not attack the family or marriage. Instead, she argued that women should be 'people first, and then women or men', that women should be able to develop their talents in education and work, and that the law should treat them as equal citizens.

This moderation was a strategy as well as a belief. Under martial law, openly radical arguments could be treated as political subversion. By framing feminism around fairness, education and the modern economy, Lu could reach educated middle-class women through essays, talks and a small publishing operation. Historians often describe this as the founding of modern feminist thinking in Taiwan, and as the first organized women's-rights effort, starting around 1972.

The idea that grew from this period is that women's equality in Taiwan would be won mainly through law. Later activists kept that focus: they drafted bills, lobbied legislators and brought constitutional challenges. This is one of the clearest differences between Taiwan's movement and, for example, the American second wave, which put more energy into consciousness-raising groups and cultural critique.

Lu was also active in the democracy movement known as the Tangwai, meaning 'outside the party'. After the Kaohsiung Incident in December 1979, a human-rights rally that ended in clashes with police, she was arrested with other opposition leaders and sentenced by a military court. She spent about five and a half years in prison and was released in 1985. Her imprisonment showed how closely feminism and democracy were tied together in Taiwan.

With Lu in prison, the work passed to her associates. Lee Yuan-chen, who had studied Chinese literature at National Taiwan University and become familiar with Western feminist writing, led a group that founded the Awakening publishing house and its monthly magazine, Awakening (婦女新知), in 1982. For the rest of the 1980s it was the only independent group publicly campaigning for gender equality. The magazine published essays on women's work, sexuality, marriage and the law, and it gave a generation of women writers a place to think in public.

When martial law ended in July 1987, civic life opened very quickly. In November 1987 Awakening became the Awakening Foundation. That same year two events showed the range of issues the movement would take on. Fifty-seven women working at the National Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall in Taipei hired lawyers to fight rules that required them to leave their jobs at age 30 or when they became pregnant. And the Huaxi Street march in Taipei protested the trafficking of young girls, many of them Indigenous, into prostitution.

sections.title: Two cases that changed public opinion

blocks.text: Laws are usually passed when a problem becomes impossible to ignore. In the 1990s, two cases made violence against women impossible to ignore in Taiwan.

The first was the case of Deng Ru-wen. In late 1993 in Banqiao, in what is now New Taipei, Deng killed her husband after years of severe abuse by him. Under the law at the time, she had very few ways to protect herself: there were no civil protection orders, and police and courts tended to treat violence inside the home as a private family matter. Women's groups, human-rights groups and the opposition DPP's women's committee rallied to support her. She was sentenced to three years in prison, a far lighter sentence than a homicide normally brought. The case raised a hard question in public: if the law offered an abused wife no protection, what was she supposed to do?

The second case was the disappearance of Peng Wan-ru, the director of the DPP's women's affairs department, on the night of 30 November 1996 in Kaohsiung. She was last seen getting into a taxi after a party meeting. That same day, the party congress approved her proposal that a quarter of its elected seats be reserved for women. She was found murdered days later. The case was never solved; the statute of limitations ran out in 2016. Her death, together with other violent crimes, brought tens of thousands of people into the streets in May 1997 to demand better protection for women and for public safety.

These cases connected the private and the public. One showed that violence at home was a matter for the state. The other showed that a woman could be killed simply by trying to get home safely at night. Together they gave feminist groups the public support they needed to pass laws they had already been drafting.

sections.title: Rewriting the law, one statute at a time

blocks.text: Family law came first. In 1994 the Council of Grand Justices, Taiwan's constitutional court, issued Interpretation No. 365. It ruled that the Civil Code clause giving fathers the final say over children violated the constitution's guarantee of equality between men and women. The legislature then revised the custody rules in 1996, so that courts would decide custody based on the best interests of the child rather than defaulting to the father. Further reforms in the following years changed the rules on marital property and residence.

Laws on violence followed. A law on preventing sexual assault was passed in 1997. On 24 June 1998, the Legislative Yuan passed the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (家庭暴力防治法). It allowed victims to apply to courts for protection orders, which could order an abuser to stay away, to move out of the home or to attend treatment. It required local governments to set up domestic violence prevention centers, and it made police, doctors, social workers and teachers responsible for reporting. The act is often called the first domestic violence law in Asia. That claim is disputed: Malaysia passed a Domestic Violence Act in 1994, and South Korea passed domestic violence laws in 1997. It is fair to say that Taiwan's act was among the first in Asia and was unusually comprehensive.

Work and school came next. Awakening had drafted a gender equality in employment bill in 1989. It finally passed in 2001 and took effect in 2002, banning discrimination in hiring, pay, promotion and dismissal, outlawing rules like the ones the Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall workers had fought, and creating rights to parental leave. In 2004 the Gender Equity Education Act required schools to teach gender equity and to protect students regardless of gender, gender identity or sexual orientation. That act was shaped by the death in April 2000 of Yeh Yung-chih, a gender-nonconforming junior high student who had been bullied and was found dying in a school bathroom.

Taiwan's feminists did not always agree. The sharpest split came in 1997, when Taipei's mayor at the time, Chen Shui-bian, abolished the city's system of licensed prostitution. Some feminists supported abolition as a way to protect women from exploitation. Others, including activists associated with the sex-workers' movement, argued that ending licences took away the livelihood and legal standing of the licensed women without giving them anything in return. The debate was framed as a conflict between 'sexual liberation' and 'sexual critique', and it divided activists for years.

By the late 1990s the movement had also widened. Groups began working on the division of household labour, the decriminalization of adultery, the rights of immigrant wives from Southeast Asia and China, and LGBTQ rights. The Awakening Foundation itself marched in Taiwan's early Pride parades. Some critics argued that a legal strategy helped educated, middle-class women most and did less for factory workers, immigrant spouses and Indigenous women. Supporters answered that laws such as the Domestic Violence Prevention Act protect everyone, including the women who have the least power.

sections.title: What was happening elsewhere in East Asia

blocks.text: South Korea followed a similar path, because its movement also grew alongside democratization. The Korea Women's Hotline was founded in 1983 to help victims of domestic violence, and after the country's democratic transition in 1987 women's groups pushed through domestic violence laws in 1997, a year before Taiwan's.

Japan democratized much earlier but moved more slowly on these issues. It passed its Equal Employment Opportunity Law in 1985, after ratifying the UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, but the law was widely criticized as weak in its early years. Japan's domestic violence law came in 2001, three years after Taiwan's.

Taiwan's situation was unusual in one respect. Because it was excluded from the United Nations after 1971, it could not formally ratify UN human-rights treaties. Its women's rights laws were therefore driven mainly by domestic activists and court rulings rather than by international treaty obligations. Taiwan later adopted CEDAW into domestic law by its own legislation in 2011.

Annette Lu became vice president in 2000, and Tsai Ing-wen was elected Taiwan's first woman president in 2016. International indices now rank Taiwan as one of the most gender-equal places in Asia; one ranking based on the UN's Gender Inequality Index placed it sixth in the world in 2019. Women's share of seats in the Legislative Yuan has grown steadily, helped by quota rules of the kind Peng Wan-ru fought for.

Many of the laws from this period are still being amended. The Domestic Violence Prevention Act has been revised several times, including to cover violence in dating relationships. The Gender Equity Education Act became part of the background to the long debate that led to same-sex marriage in 2019. For anyone interested in Taiwan's social issues today, much of the legal framework for women's safety, children's education and LGBTQ students goes back to the decisions activists made between 1987 and 2004.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: Taiwan's movement chose to work mainly through law and lobbying rather than through cultural protest. What did that choice make possible, and which women's problems are hardest to solve through a new statute alone?

glossary.explain: Taiwanese lawyer and politician who founded modern feminist thinking in Taiwan in the early 1970s, was jailed after the 1979 Kaohsiung Incident, and served as vice president from 2000 to 2008.
Annette Lu's 1970s feminist program, which argued for women's equality in education, work and law in moderate terms suited to martial-law Taiwan.
Scholar of Chinese literature and a leading feminist of the 1980s who co-founded the Awakening publishing house and magazine in 1982.
Feminist magazine founded in 1982 that became the Awakening Foundation in November 1987, Taiwan's leading feminist advocacy group.
The pro-democracy opposition movement of the 1970s and 1980s, meaning 'outside the party', which later formed the DPP.
A December 1979 human-rights rally in Kaohsiung that ended in clashes, after which opposition leaders including Annette Lu were imprisoned.
Emergency rule in Taiwan from 1949 to July 1987 that restricted parties, the press and civic groups.
Woman who killed her abusive husband in Banqiao in late 1993; her case made domestic violence a national issue.
Head of the DPP women's affairs department who was murdered after disappearing in Kaohsiung on 30 November 1996; her case remains unsolved.
A 1994 constitutional ruling that the Civil Code's preference for fathers in decisions about children violated gender equality.
Taiwan's 1998 law that created civil protection orders and local domestic violence prevention centers.
A court order that can require an abuser to stay away, leave the home or attend treatment.
Law passed in 2001 and in force from 2002 that bans sex discrimination at work and creates parental leave rights.
2004 law requiring gender equity education and protection for students of every gender identity and sexual orientation.
Gender-nonconforming junior high student who died in a school bathroom in April 2000; his death shaped the 2004 education act.
A 1987 protest in Taipei against the trafficking of young girls into prostitution.
Taiwan's main body of private law, whose family chapters long gave husbands and fathers priority.
Taiwan's first woman president, elected in 2016.
Taipei mayor who abolished licensed prostitution in 1997, later president from 2000 to 2008.
